newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico petrochem plan seeks investment, not revenue.
newsitem.headline: Mexico petrochem plan seeks investment, not revenue.

text.p: Mexico's top priority in its new scheme for privatising the petrochemical industry is to attract up to $5 billion in private investment rather than to raise revenue for the government, Energy Minister Jesus Reyes Heroles told Reuters in an interview.

Reyes Heroles described the compromise scheme as "an advance" for the government because it offered a way out of a tricky impasse, though he conceded that it was largely forced by pressure from the oil workers' union.
"The worst thing we could have done was to continue as we were" in a stalemate over the privatisation, he said. "The cost to the petrochemical sector was terrible."

Bowing to fierce union and political opposition, the government announced Sunday it was scrapping an earlier scheme to sell off 100 percent of 61 secondary petrochemical plants owned by state oil giant Pemex.

Instead, it said, private investors would be offered up to 49 percent of existing plant, but would be free to take 100 percent of new projects. Nine basic petrochemical products would be reserved solely for the state in perpetuity.
Asked why the government did not override the union and sell off all 100 percent as planned, Reyes Heroles said incredulously: "Do you really think we could have done that ?"
The much-delayed petrochemical privatisation was originally announced in January 1995 as a tool to raise around $1.5 billion in revenue for public finances.

But Reyes Heroles said most of the cash raised by the sale of minority stakes would now be used by Pemex to eliminate bottlenecks, increase capacity and carry out major maintenance at some of the crumbling existing petrochemical complexes.
He did not give a target figure for the amount to be raised, but his staff noted that the total book value of the 61 plants totalled $6 billion and was "certainly overvalued".

A more realistic figure for income from sales of minority stakes might be around $500 million, ministry sources said -- about the same figure Pemex needed to invest in de-bottlenecking and overhauling the plants.
"For four years there has been no money invested in the fundamental (petrochemical) plants", Reyes Heroles said.

Initial ventures were likely to see private capital buying into existing plant and thus financing debottling and other operating improvements, rather than the construction of greenfield sites, Reyes Heroles added.
The new mixed private-public petrochemical units would be run as commercial ventures, he said.

"New investors will be able to set conditions, such as saying they will invest 49 percent subject to a business plan to remove bottlenecks," Reyes Heroles said. "This would be a contractual commitment backed by common law."

Advantages investors would gain by buying into existing plants would include a saving of time and smaller risk, as well as a voice in the management board, Reyes Heroles said. Buyers were likely to be major clients for the products made who wanted to guarantee supply and price.

He said not all of the new subsidiaries would be sold the same way and added that sale methods were still under discussion, though no group (such as workers) would receive priority in allocations. No actual sales of shares were likely until next year, because the law needed to be changed first.

Future strategy was for Pemex Petrochemicals to gradually cede market share to new private competitors, Reyes Heroles said. "We are not going to build more plants," he said. "We won't grow (Pemex Petrochemicals) any more".
Pemex had identified new petrochemical projects for private sector funding worth $1.06 billion, he said.

The state giant planned to spend $400 to $500 million on improving and debottlenecking existing facilities -- using money raised by share sales or on international markets -- and the private sector had talked of projects in various stages of seriousness worth a total of $3.7 billion, he added.

Some commentators have expressed doubt over whether anyone would be interested in being a minority partner with Pemex but Reyes Heroles said Mexican and foreign companies were "desperate to invest" in petrochemicals here and confidently predicted success for the new scheme. In the unlikely event of failure, he added: "I'll lose my job."
